warmup.q: record Quote(String pair, List<BigDecimal> tiers) {}. A caller builds it from an ArrayList, then adds an element to that same ArrayList. What does quote.tiers() show?
options: The original elements: records are immutable
The new element too: the record holds the caller's list
It throws UnsupportedOperationException when the caller adds
It depends on whether the record was built with new
warmup.why: A record's fields are final, so tiers will always point to the same list. But it's the caller's list, and nothing stops the caller from changing it. Records are shallowly immutable. To make the quote really immutable, copy the list in a compact constructor with List.copyOf.

sections.html:
The surest way to avoid a race is to have nothing to race on. If no thread can change an object after it is built, every thread can read it at any time, with no lock, no volatile and no atomics. Lesson 3 of this track listed "don't share" as the first fix to reach for. This lesson is about that fix.

An object is immutable when all its fields are final and set in the constructor, it has no setters, every mutable thing it holds is copied in and never handed out, and this doesn't escape during construction. Records and Kotlin data classes with vals get you most of the way:

Java
public record Merchant(String id, int feeBps, Currency settlementCurrency) {   // fields are final

    public Merchant withFeeBps(int newFee) {             // "changes" return a new object
        return new Merchant(id, newFee, settlementCurrency);
    }
}
Kotlin
data class Merchant(val id: String, val feeBps: Int, val settlementCurrency: Currency)   // vals: final fields

val cheaper = merchant.copy(feeBps = 180)                // "changes" return a new object

final fields also carry a guarantee from the memory model (JLS 17.5). A thread that gets a reference to the object after its constructor has finished sees the correct values of its final fields, even if the reference reached it through a data race. Non-final fields have no such promise. The memory model track covers why.

The pattern that follows is the cheapest way to share data that changes now and then: keep an immutable snapshot behind a volatile reference and replace it whole.

Java
private volatile Map<String, BigDecimal> rates = Map.of();      // an immutable map, replaced whole

void refresh(Map<String, BigDecimal> fresh) {
    rates = Map.copyOf(fresh);                 // build it completely, then publish it in one write
}

BigDecimal rate(String pair) {
    return rates.get(pair);                    // no lock: every map this field ever points to is immutable
}
Kotlin
@Volatile private var rates: Map<String, BigDecimal> = emptyMap()   // an immutable map, replaced whole

fun refresh(fresh: Map<String, BigDecimal>) {
    rates = java.util.Map.copyOf(fresh)        // build it completely, then publish it in one write
}

fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal? = rates[pair]   // no lock: every map this field ever points to is immutable

This is the FX cache from lesson 7 of this track without any lock. The refresher builds the new map off to the side, where no reader can see it, and publishes it with one volatile write. A reader that reads the field once sees one complete version. If a reader needs several values from the same version, it copies the reference into a local first and reads them all from that.

try.title: Half-done refreshes, counted
steps: Read SnapshotSwap. A refresher moves four FX rates to a new version over and over. It updates a ConcurrentHashMap in place, and also publishes an immutable snapshot through a volatile field.
For one second, the main thread reads all four rates from each and counts reads that saw two versions at once. Predict both counts.

code.title: SnapshotSwap.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l11; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; /** * An FX rate table refreshed as a whole while readers price payments. Every refresh moves all * rates to the same new "version". A reader that sees two versions in one quote saw a half-done refresh. */ public class SnapshotSwap { static final String[] PAIRS = {"EURUSD", "GBPUSD", "USDJPY", "USDCHF"}; // 1. shared mutable map, refreshed in place (each put is thread-safe on its own) static final Map<String, Long> live = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // 2. an immutable map behind a volatile reference, replaced in one write static volatile Map<String, Long> snapshot = Map.of(); static volatile boolean done; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread refresher = new Thread(() -> { for (long version = 1; !done; version++) { for (String p : PAIRS) live.put(p, version); // readers can see a mix Map<String, Long> fresh = new HashMap<>(); for (String p : PAIRS) fresh.put(p, version); snapshot = Map.copyOf(fresh); // build fully, then publish once } }); refresher.start(); long mixedLive = 0, mixedSnapshot = 0, reads = 0; long end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { reads++; if (mixed(live)) mixedLive++; if (mixed(snapshot)) mixedSnapshot++; // one read of the reference: one version } done = true; refresher.join(); System.out.printf("reads: %,d mixed versions, shared mutable map: %,d immutable snapshot: %d%n", reads, mixedLive, mixedSnapshot); } static boolean mixed(Map<String, Long> rates) { Long first = rates.get(PAIRS[0]); for (String p : PAIRS) if (!java.util.Objects.equals(rates.get(p), first)) return true; return false; } }

alt.title: SnapshotSwap.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l11 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import kotlin.concurrent.thread // An FX rate table refreshed as a whole while readers price payments. Every refresh moves all // rates to the same new "version". A reader that sees two versions in one quote saw a half-done refresh. private val PAIRS = listOf("EURUSD", "GBPUSD", "USDJPY", "USDCHF") // 1. shared mutable map, refreshed in place (each put is thread-safe on its own) private val live = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long>() // 2. an immutable map behind a volatile reference, replaced in one write @Volatile private var snapshot: Map<String, Long> = emptyMap() @Volatile private var done = false private fun mixed(rates: Map<String, Long>): Boolean { val first = rates[PAIRS[0]] return PAIRS.any { rates[it] != first } } fun main() { val refresher = thread { var version = 1L while (!done) { for (p in PAIRS) live[p] = version // readers can see a mix snapshot = java.util.Map.copyOf(PAIRS.associateWith { version }) // build fully, then publish once version++ } } var mixedLive = 0L; var mixedSnapshot = 0L; var reads = 0L val end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L while (System.nanoTime() < end) { reads++ if (mixed(live)) mixedLive++ if (mixed(snapshot)) mixedSnapshot++ // one read of the reference: one version } done = true refresher.join() println("reads: %,d mixed versions, shared mutable map: %,d immutable snapshot: %d".format(reads, mixedLive, mixedSnapshot)) }

try.expect: The shared mutable map shows mixed versions in hundreds of thousands of reads (271,876 of 1,422,759 in one run here), although every single put and get was thread-safe. The immutable snapshot shows 0, every run.

sections.h: Records and data classes are only shallowly immutable
sections.html:
final freezes the reference, not the object behind it. A record that stores a caller's ArrayList or byte[] can change whenever the caller changes it, and so can anyone you hand the array to. The lab's FxQuote has exactly this problem. The fix is a defensive copy: copy mutable things on the way in, and, for arrays, on the way out too.

Java
public record Settlement(String merchantId, List<Payment> payments) {
    public Settlement {
        payments = List.copyOf(payments);      // reassign the parameter: the field gets the copy
    }
}
Kotlin
class Settlement(val merchantId: String, payments: List<Payment>) {
    val payments: List<Payment> = java.util.List.copyOf(payments)   // a plain parameter, copied into a property
}

A few details decide whether the copy works.

List.copyOf makes an unmodifiable copy: later changes to the source don't show, and add on the copy throws. Collections.unmodifiableList(list) is not a copy. It is a read-only view of the caller's list, so the caller's later changes show straight through it.

Arrays can't be made read-only. Clone in the constructor, and clone again in the accessor, or keep the data in an immutable type instead.

Elements must be immutable too. A copied list of mutable Payment objects is a new list of the same shared objects.

Kotlin adds one trap of its own. List is a read-only interface, not an immutable list: a data class with val tiers: List<Tier> stores whatever MutableList the caller passed, and Java code, or a cast, can still change it. A data class also can't copy its constructor parameters, because those parameters are its properties. Use a plain class, as above, when you need the copy.

In Java, BigDecimal, String, Instant, LocalDate, UUID and the boxed numbers are immutable already. Date, Calendar and arrays are not.

try.title: Mutate a record from outside
steps: Read ShallowRecord. ShallowQuote keeps the caller's list and array; DeepQuote copies them in and out. A third reference is an unmodifiableList view.
After construction, the caller changes its list and array, and a reader writes into the array it got from signature(). Predict all three lines.
Run it, then run the Kotlin twin, which adds one more line.

code.title: ShallowRecord.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l11; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; /** A record's fields are final. The objects they point to are not. */ public class ShallowRecord { record ShallowQuote(String pair, List<String> tiers, byte[] signature) {} record DeepQuote(String pair, List<String> tiers, byte[] signature) { DeepQuote { tiers = List.copyOf(tiers); // copy in signature = signature.clone(); } @Override public byte[] signature() { return signature.clone(); // copy out } } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> tiers = new ArrayList<>(List.of("up to 10k at 1.0842")); byte[] sig = {7, 7, 7}; ShallowQuote shallow = new ShallowQuote("EURUSD", tiers, sig); DeepQuote deep = new DeepQuote("EURUSD", tiers, sig); List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(tiers); // a read-only VIEW, not a copy tiers.add("above 10k at 9.9999"); // the caller keeps changing its list... sig[0] = 0; // ...and its array shallow.signature()[1] = 0; // a reader scribbles on what it was given deep.signature()[1] = 0; System.out.println("shallow: " + shallow.tiers() + " signature " + Arrays.toString(shallow.signature())); System.out.println("deep: " + deep.tiers() + " signature " + Arrays.toString(deep.signature())); System.out.println("unmodifiableList view: " + view); } }

alt.title: ShallowRecord.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l11 // A data class's vals can't be reassigned. The objects they point to can still change. private data class LooseQuote(val pair: String, val tiers: List<String>, val signature: ByteArray) private class SealedQuote(val pair: String, tiers: List<String>, signature: ByteArray) { val tiers: List<String> = java.util.List.copyOf(tiers) // copy in: unmodifiable even through a cast private val sig = signature.copyOf() val signature: ByteArray get() = sig.copyOf() // copy out } fun main() { val tiers = mutableListOf("up to 10k at 1.0842") val sig = byteArrayOf(7, 7, 7) val loose = LooseQuote("EURUSD", tiers, sig) // List<String> is read-only, not immutable val sealed = SealedQuote("EURUSD", tiers, sig) val view = java.util.Collections.unmodifiableList(tiers) // a read-only VIEW, not a copy tiers.add("above 10k at 9.9999") // the caller keeps changing its list... sig[0] = 0 // ...and its array loose.signature[1] = 0 // a reader scribbles on what it was given sealed.signature[1] = 0 println("shallow: ${loose.tiers} signature ${loose.signature.contentToString()}") println("deep: ${sealed.tiers} signature ${sealed.signature.contentToString()}") println("unmodifiableList view: $view") (loose.tiers as MutableList<String>).add("added through a cast") // read-only interface, mutable object println("shallow after a cast: ${loose.tiers}") }

try.expect: The shallow quote shows the extra tier and a signature of [0, 0, 7]: both the caller and a reader changed it. The deep quote still shows one tier and [7, 7, 7]. The unmodifiableList view shows the extra tier, because it's a view. In Kotlin, a cast to MutableList adds to the shallow quote's "read-only" list.

sections.h: Confinement keeps mutable state on one thread
sections.html:
Mutable state is fine as long as only one thread can reach it. That is confinement, and you already use it every day.

Stack confinement is the simplest: local variables live on one thread's stack. A StringBuilder or ArrayList created inside a method and never stored anywhere else needs no protection at all.

Java
String statementLine(Payment p) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();      // local: no other thread can ever see it
    sb.append(p.id()).append(';').append(p.cents());
    return sb.toString();                        // only the immutable String leaves
}
Kotlin
fun statementLine(p: Payment): String = buildString {   // the builder is local: no other thread can see it
    append(p.id).append(';').append(p.cents)
}                                                        // only the immutable String leaves

Thread confinement is the same idea at a larger scale: one thread owns some state, and every other thread asks that thread to act on it. A Kafka consumer is the classic case. Each partition is read by one consumer thread at a time, so per-partition state such as the last processed offset or a running total can live in a plain HashMap that only that thread touches. Event loops work the same way.

When work moves between threads, move ownership with it. A request thread builds a batch, puts it into a BlockingQueue, and never touches it again. The writer thread takes it and owns it from then on.

Java
List<Entry> batch = new ArrayList<>();          // owned by this thread
fill(batch);
queue.put(batch);                               // ownership moves to whoever takes it
// from here on, this thread never touches batch again
Kotlin
val batch = ArrayList<Entry>()                  // owned by this thread
fill(batch)
queue.put(batch)                                // ownership moves to whoever takes it
// from here on, this thread never touches batch again

The queue does two jobs. It hands the object over, and it makes the hand-off visible: everything the producer did before put happens-before the consumer's take returns. The figure shows the moment ownership changes. The rule is all on the producer: once you've handed it over, it isn't yours. A producer that reuses the list for the next batch is sharing a mutable object with no synchronization at all, and the writer sees half-cleared batches.

try.title: Hand over, or keep using?
steps: Read HandOff. A producer fills 5,000 batches of 100 entries and puts each into a queue. A writer thread checks that every batch it takes is complete and in order.
Run it. Then run it with -Pargs=reuse, where the producer clears and refills one list instead of creating a new one.
Run the reuse version a few times. Is the damage count the same each time?

code.title: HandOff.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l11; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; /** * A request thread fills batches of 100 ledger entries and hands each one to a writer thread * through a queue. Run with -Pargs=reuse to reuse one list instead of handing over a new one. */ public class HandOff { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean reuse = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("reuse"); BlockingQueue<List<Integer>> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(4); int batches = 5_000; int[] damaged = {0}; Thread writer = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int b = 0; b < batches; b++) { List<Integer> batch = queue.take(); // the writer owns this list now try { Object[] entries = batch.toArray(); boolean ok = entries.length == 100; for (int i = 0; ok && i < 100; i++) ok = entries[i].equals(((Integer) entries[0]) + i); if (!ok) damaged[0]++; } catch (RuntimeException e) { damaged[0]++; // a list changing under you can throw, too } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "ledger-writer"); writer.start(); List<Integer> shared = new ArrayList<>(); for (int b = 0; b < batches; b++) { List<Integer> batch = reuse ? shared : new ArrayList<>(100); batch.clear(); // with reuse: clears a list the writer may be reading for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) batch.add(b * 100 + i); queue.put(batch); // hand it over, and never touch it again } writer.join(); System.out.printf("%s: %,d batches handed over, %,d damaged%n", reuse ? "reused list" : "new list each time", batches, damaged[0]); } }

alt.title: HandOff.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l11 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A request thread fills batches of 100 ledger entries and hands each one to a writer thread // through a queue. Run with -Pargs=reuse to reuse one list instead of handing over a new one. fun main(args: Array<String>) { val reuse = args.firstOrNull() == "reuse" val queue = ArrayBlockingQueue<MutableList<Int>>(4) val batches = 5_000 var damaged = 0 val writer = thread(name = "ledger-writer") { repeat(batches) { val batch = queue.take() // the writer owns this list now try { val entries = batch.toTypedArray() val ok = entries.size == 100 && entries.indices.all { i -> entries[i] == entries[0] + i } if (!ok) damaged++ } catch (e: RuntimeException) { damaged++ // a list changing under you can throw, too } } } val shared = ArrayList<Int>() for (b in 0 until batches) { val batch = if (reuse) shared else ArrayList(100) batch.clear() // with reuse: clears a list the writer may be reading for (i in 0 until 100) batch.add(b * 100 + i) queue.put(batch) // hand it over, and never touch it again } writer.join() println("%s: %,d batches handed over, %,d damaged".format(if (reuse) "reused list" else "new list each time", batches, damaged)) }

try.expect: With a new list each time: 0 damaged batches. With reuse: some batches arrive damaged (from about a dozen to a few hundred in runs here), and the count changes every run. A lucky run could even show 0, which is exactly why this bug survives testing.

sections.h: ThreadLocal gives each thread its own copy, and pools keep it forever
sections.html:
ThreadLocal<T> gives every thread its own value for the same variable. It has two common uses: a per-thread copy of an object that isn't thread-safe, and request context, such as the tenant or user, that deep code reads without passing it around. Logging MDC, the per-request fields your logger adds to every line, is usually a ThreadLocal underneath.

The catch is where the value lives. Each Thread object has its own small map from ThreadLocal to value, and get() looks in the current thread's map. The Javadoc says a thread keeps its copy as long as the thread is alive. Pool threads live for days, and so does whatever you left on them. A value set for one request is still there when the same thread serves the next one. If the next request sets nothing, it runs as the previous customer. That's a data leak between merchants, in a payment system. The rule has no exceptions: set it, then remove it in finally.

Java
private static final ThreadLocal<String> TENANT = new ThreadLocal<>();

void handle(Request r) {
    TENANT.set(r.tenant());
    try {
        process(r);                  // deep code calls TENANT.get()
    } finally {
        TENANT.remove();             // the pool thread goes back clean
    }
}
Kotlin
private val TENANT = ThreadLocal<String>()

fun handle(r: Request) {
    TENANT.set(r.tenant)
    try {
        process(r)                   // deep code calls TENANT.get()
    } finally {
        TENANT.remove()              // the pool thread goes back clean
    }
}

Call remove(), not set(null). remove() deletes the thread's entry; set(null) keeps an entry that holds null.

For non-thread-safe helpers, prefer an immutable replacement over a per-thread copy. DateTimeFormatter is immutable, so one shared instance replaces a ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat>. Per-thread copies also scale badly with virtual threads, where every task is a new thread with an empty copy. The virtual threads track goes into that.

For request context, JDK 25 made scoped values final (JEP 506). A scoped value is bound for the duration of one call and is gone when the call returns, so there is nothing to forget:

Java
static final ScopedValue<String> TENANT = ScopedValue.newInstance();   // JDK 25+

void handle(Request r) {
    ScopedValue.where(TENANT, r.tenant()).run(() -> process(r));   // bound for this call only
}
Kotlin
val TENANT: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance()            // JDK 25+

fun handle(r: Request) {
    ScopedValue.where(TENANT, r.tenant).run { process(r) }          // bound for this call only
}

That code needs JDK 25 or later; on JDK 21 to 24 the API is a preview, so the labs, which compile for JDK 21, use ThreadLocal.

try.title: Watch one customer's context leak into another's request
steps: Read ThreadLocalBleed. Six requests run one after another on a pool of one thread. The handler sets the user only when the request carries one.
Predict what each request without a user runs as, in the leaky version and in the clean one.

code.title: ThreadLocalBleed.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l11; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.function.Function; /** * Six requests on a pool of one reused thread. The handler sets the user only when the request * carries one. A pool of 1 makes the bug happen every time; a pool of 200 makes it rare and random. */ public class ThreadLocalBleed { static final ThreadLocal<String> USER = new ThreadLocal<>(); static String leaky(String user) { if (user != null) USER.set(user); return "request(" + user + ") ran as " + USER.get(); } static String clean(String user) { if (user != null) USER.set(user); try { return "request(" + user + ") ran as " + USER.get(); } finally { USER.remove(); // leave the thread as you found it } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String[] requests = {"alice", null, "bob", null, null, "carol"}; for (Function<String, String> handler : java.util.List.<Function<String, String>>of(ThreadLocalBleed::leaky, ThreadLocalBleed::clean)) { ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); System.out.println("---"); for (String user : requests) System.out.println(" " + pool.submit(() -> handler.apply(user)).get()); pool.shutdown(); } } }

alt.title: ThreadLocalBleed.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l11 import java.util.concurrent.Executors // Six requests on a pool of one reused thread. The handler sets the user only when the request // carries one. A pool of 1 makes the bug happen every time; a pool of 200 makes it rare and random. private val USER = ThreadLocal<String>() private fun leaky(user: String?): String { if (user != null) USER.set(user) return "request($user) ran as ${USER.get()}" } private fun clean(user: String?): String { if (user != null) USER.set(user) try { return "request($user) ran as ${USER.get()}" } finally { USER.remove() // leave the thread as you found it } } fun main() { val requests = listOf("alice", null, "bob", null, null, "carol") for (handler in listOf(::leaky, ::clean)) { val pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor() println("---") for (user in requests) println(" " + pool.submit<String> { handler(user) }.get()) pool.shutdown() } }

try.expect: Leaky: the first anonymous request runs as alice, and the next two run as bob, whoever that thread served last. Clean: every anonymous request runs as null, because remove() in finally put the thread back as it was. A pool of one makes it happen every time. With 200 threads it happens rarely and randomly, which is how it reaches production.

analogy: An immutable object is a printed price list: anyone can read it at the same time, and to change a price you print a new list and swap it on the wall. Confinement is a ledger kept in one clerk's desk; others pass notes to that clerk instead of writing in it. A hand-off through a queue is passing a folder across the counter: once it's handed over, you don't reach back to add a page. A ThreadLocal on a pool thread is a locker that the next shift inherits, with whatever the last person left in it, unless someone empties it at the end of every shift. The analogy breaks at the price list: a printed list can't be edited by a stranger, but a Java object with one unprotected List field can.
world: Kafka already confines state for you: one partition is read by one consumer thread at a time, so per-partition state needs no locks, as long as you don't hand it to another thread. Events and commands on the bus should be immutable records, so a consumer can pass them to a worker pool without copying. Temporal runs a workflow's code one thread at a time, so workflow state is confined by design; activities run on an ordinary thread pool and get none of that protection. And look at every ThreadLocal in your Quarkus services, including the ones inside libraries: logging MDC, a tenant or merchant context, a security principal. Each one needs a finally that clears it, or a framework hook that does it for you. A merchant id that leaks from one request into the next is a reportable incident, not just a bug.
mistake: The most common mistake is setting a ThreadLocal and never clearing it, usually because the code was written and tested where each request seemed to get a fresh thread. On a pool, the value stays on the thread. The next request that doesn't set it reads the previous request's tenant, user or MDC fields, and the logs show one customer's id on another customer's payment. Unit tests rarely catch it, because each test usually runs on a fresh thread or in a fresh JVM. The fix is mechanical: every set is paired with a remove() in a finally, or replaced by a scoped value on JDK 25 and later. The lab's TenantScope goes one step further and restores the previous value, so nested calls work too.

compare.title: A deeply immutable value in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java record
java.html: public record Settlement(String merchantId, List<Payment> payments) { public Settlement { payments = List.copyOf(payments); // reassign the parameter: the field gets the copy } }

kotlin.title: Kotlin class
kotlin.html: class Settlement(val merchantId: String, payments: List<Payment>) { val payments: List<Payment> = java.util.List.copyOf(payments) // a plain parameter, copied into a property } // a data class can't do this: its constructor parameters ARE the properties

compare.note: Both compile to a class with final fields, so both get the memory model's final-field guarantee. The difference is where the copy can go. A Java record's compact constructor may reassign its parameters before the fields are set, so payments = List.copyOf(payments) stores the copy. A Kotlin data class can't do that, because its primary-constructor parameters are the properties, so you use a plain class with a separate property, as here, or a private constructor and a factory. Kotlin's List type doesn't help as much as it looks: it's a read-only interface, and listOf or toList results can still be changed through a cast or from Java. java.util.List.copyOf gives you a list that is unmodifiable for everyone. Data class copy() is shallow too: the copy shares the same list.

worked.title: A shared constant that someone changed

steps.say: A payment service adds a card fee to every order. Money looks like a value, and CARD_FEE looks like a constant. Read it and find what changes, and for whom.
steps.code: public class Money { private long cents; private final Currency currency; public Money(long cents, Currency currency) { this.cents = cents; this.currency = currency; } public Money add(Money other) { // changes this object, then returns it this.cents += other.cents; return this; } public long cents() { return cents; } } static final Money CARD_FEE = new Money(30, EUR); // "a constant" Money total = order.amount().add(CARD_FEE); // also changes order.amount()

alt.html: class Money(private var centsValue: Long, val currency: Currency) { fun add(other: Money): Money { // changes this object, then returns it centsValue += other.centsValue return this } val cents: Long get() = centsValue } val CARD_FEE = Money(30, EUR) // "a constant" val total = order.amount.add(CARD_FEE) // also changes order.amount

steps.say: add changes the object it's called on. The line order.amount().add(CARD_FEE) changes the order's own amount. Somewhere else, CARD_FEE.add(surcharge) changes the fee for every request on every thread. And because cents is neither final nor volatile, other threads may see the old fee, the new one, or a mix, at different times. static final on the reference didn't make the object constant.
Make Money a value: final fields, and operations that return a new instance. Now CARD_FEE can be read by 200 threads with no lock, and nobody can change it.
steps.code: public record Money(long cents, Currency currency) { public Money { Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency"); } public Money plus(Money other) { // 1. never change this; return a new value if (!currency.equals(other.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch"); return new Money(Math.addExact(cents, other.cents), currency); // 2. overflow fails loudly } }

alt.html: data class Money(val cents: Long, val currency: Currency) { operator fun plus(other: Money): Money { // 1. never change this; return a new value require(currency == other.currency) { "currency mismatch" } return copy(cents = Math.addExact(cents, other.cents)) // 2. overflow fails loudly } }

steps.say: Before reading on, explain to yourself why the record version needs no synchronization even though CARD_FEE is read by every request thread. Then look at the classic trap with immutable types, which catches people moving from mutable ones: calling the operation and ignoring the result.
steps.code: BigDecimal total = BigDecimal.ZERO; for (BigDecimal fee : fees) total.add(fee); // does nothing: the result is thrown away for (BigDecimal fee : fees) total = total.add(fee); // right

alt.html: var total = BigDecimal.ZERO for (fee in fees) total.add(fee) // does nothing: the result is thrown away for (fee in fees) total += fee // right: plus() returns a new BigDecimal

steps.say: Answer: the fields are final, set once in the constructor, and the object never changes, so every thread that can see the reference sees 30 EUR. There is nothing to race on. The price is an allocation per operation, which the JIT often removes when the object doesn't escape. For money, that trade is easy.

lab.title: A deeply immutable quote and a tenant scope that cleans up
steps: Run the tests. All six fail. The three FxQuote tests change the quote from outside, through the list you passed in, the list it returns, and its signature array. The three TenantScope tests run on a pool of one thread and find a tenant left over from an earlier call.
Give FxQuote a compact constructor that replaces tiers with List.copyOf(tiers) and signature with a clone.
Override signature() so it returns a clone, not the field.
Fix TenantScope.runAs: remember the previous value, set the new one (or remove() for null), run the work in a try, and in finally put the previous value back (or remove() if there was none).
Run the tests until all six pass.
hints: In a compact constructor you assign to the parameter (tiers = List.copyOf(tiers);), not to this.tiers. The record assigns the fields after your code runs.
List.copyOf also rejects null elements, which is usually what you want in a quote.
Restoring the previous value instead of always calling remove() makes nested calls work: an inner runAs must hand the thread back to the outer one, not wipe it.

drill.title: An immutable refund from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write an immutable Refund with a payment id, a list of line items and a reason, safe to share between threads, plus withReason(String) that returns a changed copy. Check: can the caller's list, or the list you return, change your refund?

answer.html: public record Refund(String paymentId, List<LineItem> items, String reason) { public Refund { items = List.copyOf(items); // copy in; unmodifiable for everyone } public Refund withReason(String newReason) { return new Refund(paymentId, items, newReason); // a new object, same items } }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: class Refund(val paymentId: String, items: List<LineItem>, val reason: String) { val items: List<LineItem> = java.util.List.copyOf(items) // copy in; unmodifiable for everyone fun withReason(newReason: String) = Refund(paymentId, items, newReason) // a new object, same items }

recap: An object nobody can change needs no locks. Make fields final, add no setters, copy mutable parts, and don't let this escape.
For data that changes now and then, publish an immutable snapshot through a volatile field and replace it whole.
Records and data classes are shallow. Copy lists with List.copyOf and clone arrays in and out. unmodifiableList is a view, not a copy.
Confinement: locals, one owner thread (one Kafka partition per consumer), or ownership handed through a queue and never touched again.
Every ThreadLocal.set on a pool thread needs a remove() in finally. On JDK 25+, scoped values do the cleanup for you.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to add a lock around a merchant-settings object that a refresher updates every minute and every request reads. Explain the alternative you'd suggest, and why it is safe.
explain.answer: I'd make the settings an immutable record, with final fields and copied lists, and keep the current one in a volatile field. The refresher builds a complete new settings object off to the side and then assigns it to the field in one write. Requests read the field once and use that object. It's safe because nothing a reader can reach is ever modified: the old object stays valid for whoever is still using it, and the volatile write makes the new object, including all its fields, visible to every reader that reads the field afterwards. Readers never wait, and there's no lock to forget. The one thing to watch is a reader that reads the field twice and gets two different versions, so read it into a local first.

deeper.html:
Each Thread object has its own small hash map for its thread locals, called ThreadLocalMap. The keys are weak references to the ThreadLocal objects, and the values are strong references. When a ThreadLocal itself becomes garbage, its key goes away, but the value stays in the map until a later get, set or remove on that thread happens to clean it up. On a pool thread that lives for days, that can be a long time. In application servers this is a famous leak: a value whose class came from a redeployed web application keeps that application's whole class loader alive. remove() avoids all of it.

InheritableThreadLocal copies values from a parent thread to a child thread when the child is created. It does nothing useful with pools, because pool threads are created once, long before the request that submits work to them.

Scoped values (JEP 506, final in JDK 25) fix the design problems rather than the symptoms. A binding is immutable: there is no set, so code deep in the call stack can't change the tenant under you. It has a clear lifetime: it ends when run or call returns, even on an exception. And it is cheap to share with child tasks: with structured concurrency, still a preview API in JDK 25, threads forked inside the scope see the same bindings without copying a map per thread.

One immutability trap to know: an object is only safe to share through a data race if this didn't escape while the constructor was running. A constructor that registers this as a listener, or starts a thread that uses this, hands out the object before its final fields are guaranteed to be visible. Build first, register after. The memory model track's lesson on safe publication covers the full rules.
